title: the birth
hook: in Kamsa's prison, a child is quietly moved from one mother to another, and the gods come to sing to an unborn baby

segments.voice: Yesterday the birth began at a wedding: a voice from the sky, Kamsa's sword, and Vasudeva's promise, kept. Your line was a promise made at sword point.

In the prison, Kamsa kills Devaki's children as they are born. The Bhagavata doesn't linger there. When six have died, the text says, a seventh child begins to grow in her. And this time something is done in secret. The Lord, the Bhagavata says, calls on his own power of illusion, Yogamaya, and gives her a task. A child is in danger. Move him.
screen: `A PRISON IN MATHURA.` → `THE SEVENTH CHILD.` → `"MOVE HIM."`

segments.voice: Yogamaya draws the seventh child out of Devaki's womb and places him in the womb of Rohini, another wife of Vasudeva, living safely in Gokula, a village of cowherds across the river. In the prison, people say Devaki has miscarried. In Gokula, the child grows in secret. The Bhagavata names him from that night: Sankarshana, the one who was drawn out. Later he is known as Balarama, Krishna's older brother. So the first rescue in this story is quiet and invisible. Then the Lord himself, the text says, first enters Vasudeva's mind, and from there passes into Devaki, and she begins to shine. Kamsa sees her glowing and understands: this is the one. But he can't bring himself to kill a pregnant woman, his own cousin, so he waits, and the waiting turns into obsession. Sitting, lying down, eating, walking, the text says, Kamsa saw that child everywhere. His fear made him think of the Lord constantly. And while Kamsa paces, the gods come. Brahma, Shiva and the others stand in the cell to sing praise to the child inside Devaki. Do not be afraid, mother, they tell her. The one in your womb has come to protect the world. A dark cell, a frightened mother, a jailer outside, and the whole sky gathered around someone who hasn't been born yet.
screen: `THE SEVENTH CHILD IS MOVED` · `SANKARSHANA: DRAWN OUT` · `KAMSA SEES HIM EVERYWHERE` · then, large: `THE GODS SING TO THE UNBORN CHILD`

segments.voice: Think of something good growing slowly in your life that isn't visible yet: a friendship, a skill, a healing, a child on the way. Breathe in and notice it without hurrying it; breathe out and let go of the urge to check on it, the way the gods came just to stand near what hadn't arrived. If you pray, you can hold it in your prayer.
The birth. Before it happens, a brother is moved to safety, a mother begins to shine, and the gods come to sing.
Your line: the gods come to sing. Tomorrow, midnight in the prison. See you then.

howItsDone: The prayer the gods offer to the child in Devaki's womb, told in the Bhagavata Purana's tenth book, is heard when the Bhagavata is recited, and Balarama is honored alongside Krishna in temples and festivals.

chat.says: Wait, how did Balarama end up born to a different mother?
options: Yogamaya moved him from Devaki's womb to Rohini's, safe in Gokula.
Rohini adopted him after Kamsa let the seventh baby go free.
Vasudeva carried him to Gokula the night he was born.
chat.meaning: Yogamaya drew the seventh child from Devaki's womb into Rohini's, in Gokula. He was named Sankarshana, the one drawn out.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 10.2: the six children killed, Yogamaya and the transfer of the seventh child to Rohini, the name Sankarshana, the Lord entering Vasudeva and Devaki, Kamsa's fear, the prayer of the gods

notes: All paraphrase. The count 'when six had died' follows Bhagavata 10.2 (hatesu satsu balesu); confirm.
Confirm that the text says the people spoke of a miscarriage, and that it gives the name Sankarshana for being drawn from the womb (10.2.13).

Confirm the sequence: the Lord enters Vasudeva's mind, then Devaki; Devaki's radiance; Kamsa refrains from killing a pregnant woman and thinks of Hari while sitting, lying, eating and walking (10.2.24).
The gods named as Brahma and Shiva with others; confirm. Their words to Devaki are a gloss.
The gods' prayer is known as the garbha-stuti; howItsDone describes its recitation only generally.
